title: China's first AI-generated film hits cinemas but ticket sales lag
content:
China's first AI film hits cinemas but ticket sales lag
Nearly 100 people took more than two years to make the film, which cost more than 10 million yuan (US$1.5 million).
BEIJING: China's first fully AI-generated feature film opens in cinemas on Friday (Oct 23), in what promises to be a tough box-office test for the country's booming tech industry as advance ticket sales lag.
More than 10,000 screenings of Sanxingdui: Future Past, a sci-fi thriller, are scheduled for Friday, according to ticketing platform Maoyan.
However, public reception has been less than enthusiastic.
Presale revenue as of Thursday evening stood at 65,000 yuan (US$9,700), while total box-office takings were forecast to remain below 100,000 yuan, only a fraction of the reported production cost, according to Maoyan.
Jiang Defu, CEO of the production company Bona Film Group, acknowledged the lukewarm reception in a recent interview, but said the film was pushing boundaries.
"We are the first to try it, the first to get a theatrical release permit, and the first to be tested by the audience," he told Chinese film industry outlet Yuli.
"I think that is not easy at all."
Nearly 100 people took more than two years to make the film, which cost more than 10 million yuan (US$1.5 million), Bona said.
But that was not enough to convince Iris Yang, who attended a free preview screening of the film on Thursday and said she would not have paid for a ticket, given the movie's quality.
"If AI generation can match the theatrical experience of Avatar, I think I would be willing to pay for it," Yang said, referring to the US franchise known for the quality of its animation.
AI-generated video has gained popularity in the world's second-largest economy. On Douyin, the Chinese equivalent of TikTok, AI-generated short dramas garnered more than 200 billion views in September alone.
But "the audience won't automatically pay for the tickets just because it's an AI-generated film", independent AI director Zhang Jun told AFP.
Online, Chinese social media users also seemed unconvinced by the launch of AI movies in cinemas.
"If it's free to watch on streaming platforms, it could become legendary. But paying to watch? People are not going to accept it at this stage," one user on Weibo commented.
In Hollywood, the rise of AI has sparked concern among film workers about the prospect of job losses.
An AI-generated sci-fi feature called Gods Don't Give Gifts is scheduled for US release on Dec 4.
And a virtual Hollywood actor called Tilly Norwood, whose interviews have gone viral while fuelling job fears, is also set to star in an upcoming movie called Misaligned.

report.summary: China's first fully AI-generated feature film, Sanxingdui: Future Past, opened to weak presales, testing whether audiences will pay for AI-made cinema.
report.background: China's film and tech industries have been moving quickly into generative video. AI short dramas are already a mass-market phenomenon on Douyin, where AI-generated content drew more than 200 billion views in September alone. That success encouraged producers to attempt a full-length theatrical release, not just short clips. Bona Film Group backed Sanxingdui: Future Past as a boundary-pushing project, spending over 10 million yuan and involving nearly 100 people for more than two years, showing that 'fully AI-generated' still requires substantial human labor. The release also arrives amid global debate over AI in entertainment: Hollywood workers fear job losses, an AI sci-fi feature is slated for US release in December, and a virtual actor has gone viral. China's first AI feature therefore serves as an early commercial test of whether technical novelty can translate into audience demand and sustainable business models.
key_points: Sanxingdui: Future Past opened with more than 10,000 scheduled screenings, but presale revenue was only 65,000 yuan by Thursday evening. Total box-office takings were forecast below 100,000 yuan, a tiny fraction of the reported production cost of more than 10 million yuan.

Despite being billed as fully AI-generated, the film took nearly 100 people more than two years to make. That undercuts the idea that AI instantly replaces large production teams and shows that feature-length AI filmmaking still depends on extensive human planning and post-production.

Audience skepticism is a major barrier. A preview attendee said she would not pay unless AI could match the theatrical quality of Avatar, while social media users argued AI films might work free on streaming but not as paid cinema. An AI director said audiences will not buy tickets just because a film is AI-made.

AI short-form content is booming in China, with AI-generated short dramas drawing over 200 billion views on Douyin in September. But the theatrical market demands higher visual consistency, storytelling and sound quality. Hollywood is also testing AI features and virtual actors, while film workers worry about job losses.
report.impact: The weak opening is a reality check for the AI video industry: technical novelty does not guarantee commercial demand. For AI companies and studios, it suggests near-term opportunities lie more in short-form content, advertising, previsualization and VFX assistance than in replacing full theatrical productions. Developers should focus on consistency, controllability, lip-sync, sound and narrative tools rather than chasing 'fully AI' marketing claims. For regular users, the lesson is that AI can lower production barriers, but audiences still judge films by story and spectacle. If costs fall and quality rises, AI could democratize filmmaking; if not, paid AI cinema may remain a niche experiment.
report.tools: To follow this space, watch generative-video platforms such as Kling (Kuaishou), Hailuo (MiniMax), Runway, Luma Dream Machine and Pika, which are widely used for AI short films and ads. For open-source experimentation, look at Stable Video Diffusion, AnimateDiff, Open-Sora and ComfyUI pipelines. These tools are useful for prototyping scenes and short-form content, but the film's reception shows that consistency, story and sound still need heavy human direction.
